source_title: Measurement Error Due to Patient Flow in Estimates of Intensive Care Unit Length of Stay
locator: Results, paragraph beginning 'From the administrative data'; Web Table 2
source_setting: Medical ICU, Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States.
source_period: Calendar years 2010–2012 for administrative MICU discharges; separate SUNSET-ICU trial-participant analysis, trial period not specified in this extract.
source_n: 3,851 MICU discharges for administrative analysis; Web Table 2 reports 1,149 MICU discharges among SUNSET-ICU trial participants.
quantity: Median time from observed discharge readiness to actual MICU discharge (immutable time), administrative cohort
source_evidence_basis: Observed administrative timestamps summarized by the authors; median and quartiles are measured site distributions, not modeled values.
limitations: Single academic MICU, historical 2010–2012 period, and endpoint is readiness-to-actual-departure interval rather than environmental bed-cleaning time alone. The paper calls this interval immutable time and cautions that ICU length of stay can incorporate post-readiness flow delays.
inferred_scenario_use: External proxy only: a scenario may vary a post-readiness ICU bed-occupancy delay around this reported distribution, with a separate local-calibration parameter. Do not transfer as a target-site estimate or assume all delay is caused by ward-bed unavailability.

source_title: Measurement Error Due to Patient Flow in Estimates of Intensive Care Unit Length of Stay
locator: Results, Secondary data analysis, paragraph reporting the 1,149 SUNSET-ICU discharges; the text reports the 5.1-hour median and IQR and points to Web Table 2 for percentiles. Article period is specified in Methods, Secondary data analysis.
source_setting: Medical ICU, Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States; trial-participant subset.
source_period: SUNSET-ICU MICU cohort, September 12, 2011 to September 11, 2012; ICU readmissions excluded.
source_n: 1,149 MICU discharges to another hospital unit or ward among SUNSET-ICU trial participants.
quantity: Median time from discharge readiness to actual discharge in SUNSET-ICU subset
source_evidence_basis: Observed readiness and discharge timestamps among trial participants; author-reported distribution.
limitations: Single academic MICU and trial cohort. The main Results text directly reports median 5.1 h, IQR 2.7–8.9 h, 90th percentile 14.2 h, and 95th percentile 21.7 h, citing Web Table 2; the supplementary table itself was not separately opened. Keep this cohort separate from the 2010–2012 administrative series.
inferred_scenario_use: Use only as a lower/alternate external scenario for post-readiness transfer delay; preserve separate from the 2010–2012 administrative distribution and calibrate to local timestamp definitions.

source_title: Measurement Error Due to Patient Flow in Estimates of Intensive Care Unit Length of Stay
source_setting: Medical ICU, Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States.
source_evidence_basis: Observed timestamp distribution summarized by authors; request times concentrated in the hour of morning bed-management rounds.
limitations: Single MICU workflow; reported as more than half, without an exact percentage in the article text. This is request timing, not completed transfer timing or a universal discharge schedule.
inferred_scenario_use: Can motivate a sensitivity scenario with clustered morning ICU transfer requests, while keeping local request timing unknown until measured.

source_title: Turning Over Patient Turnover: An Ethnographic Study of Admissions, Discharges, and Transfers
locator: Results, Table 1 and paragraph beginning 'There were 3562 events on the medical unit'
source_setting: One medical and one surgical inpatient unit at a U.S. hospital; institution name is not identified in the article text reviewed.
source_period: Turnover records for 2009; one year of admission/discharge records. Ethnographic fieldwork and observation took place on the two units; the paper reports 21 formal interviews among 58 nurses featured in the analysis.
source_n: Medical unit: 1,657 admissions and 1,905 discharges in 2009; 3,562 total events. Surgical unit separately had 1,893 admissions and 1,948 discharges. The source table reports events/day, but does not state the number of daily observations used for its mean.
quantity: Mean daily medical-unit turnover events (admissions plus discharges, including transfers-in/out)
source_evidence_basis: Author summary of unit-level 2009 admission and discharge records; daily event counts are observed administrative records.
limitations: One medical unit at a U.S. hospital whose name is not given in the article text reviewed; old single-year data. The table reports 9.95 events/day, but does not state the number of observed unit-days in that mean; dividing 3,562 by 365 gives about 9.76, so do not recompute or assume a 365-day denominator. Event counts do not measure duration or acuity-adjusted workload. Transfers-in are grouped with admissions and transfers-out with discharges.
inferred_scenario_use: A workload scenario may represent admissions/discharges/transfers as separate events and sample medical-unit daily event volume around this source-specific distribution; do not use as local throughput or as service minutes.

source_title: Turning Over Patient Turnover: An Ethnographic Study of Admissions, Discharges, and Transfers
locator: Results, Turnover timing; Table 3, day-to-night shift change (17:30–21:00)
source_setting: One medical and one surgical inpatient unit at a U.S. hospital; institution name is not identified in the article text reviewed.
source_n: Surgical unit: 487 of 3,841 turnover events in this interval; medical unit: 678 of 3,562 events.
quantity: Share of all unit turnover events occurring during 17:30–21:00 day-to-night shift change
source_evidence_basis: Observed administrative event timestamps tabulated by unit and time window; table shows 13% surgical and 19% medical for this interval.
limitations: Two units in one hospital and one historical year; the table percentages are rounded. Turnover events include admissions and discharges, with transfers included in those categories.
inferred_scenario_use: Can test shift-change clustering as a workload sensitivity case, preserving distinct medical and surgical profiles and requiring local event-time data for calibration.

source_title: Nurse Staffing and Inpatient Hospital Mortality
locator: Methods, Data and Population and Patient Turnover definition; Results, Characteristics of Patients, Units, and Staffing; Table 1
source_setting: 43 units at a tertiary academic medical center in the United States; adult general-care, step-down, and intensive-care units were included, with specified unit exclusions.
source_n: 197,961 admissions; 176,696 staffed unit-shifts, of 3,227,457 total patient-unit-shift records.
quantity: Observed patient turnover per staffed unit-shift; high-turnover classification frequency

value.high_turnover_rule: unit shift turnover rate >= that unit day-shift mean + 1 SD

unit: percent of shift census for turnover rate; SD in percentage points; high-turnover count and percent of staffed shifts
source_evidence_basis: Observed shift-level admissions, transfers, discharges, census, and staffing from hospital electronic systems. The article defines turnover as admissions + transfers + discharges (deaths excluded) divided by adjusted/start-of-shift census, so complete turnover equals 100%. High turnover is a shift rate >= the unit-specific day-shift mean + 1 SD; Table 1 reports 12,242 (6.9%) of 176,696 staffed shifts.
limitations: Single high-quality academic center with relatively high average staffing and lower-than-predicted mortality; historical 2003–2006. The high-turnover threshold is relative to each unit day-shift mean, not a portable absolute rate. Do not import 6.9% as a local threshold or benchmark without local calibration.
inferred_scenario_use: For sensitivity analysis only, a simulation may define high-turnover shifts using the paper’s relative rule (unit day-shift mean plus one SD) and compare the study’s observed 6.9% frequency; do not make this the target-hospital rule or infer patient outcome effects locally.
